description: We are a team of students from Simon Fraser University with shared interests in space exploration, technology, and interactive learning. Combining perspectives across engineering, technology, and project management, we collaborated to develop Orbital Architect 2D, a browser-based simulator that makes space mission design more accessible through hands-on experimentation, rocket building, and orbital navigation.
summary:
Orbital Architect 2D is an interactive, browser-based space mission design simulator that lets users build, launch, and navigate a spacecraft through a simplified planetary system. Rather than presenting space exploration as something users can only observe, the project puts them in the role of a mission designer, where every decision from engine selection and fuel capacity to staging and orbital maneuvers, affects the outcome of the mission.

Users begin in a Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB), where they can construct a multi-stage rocket using different engines, fuel tanks, and spacecraft components. The simulator calculates performance metrics, including total delta-v, thrust-to-weight ratio, mass, and fuel requirements. Once the rocket is ready, users can launch it into a two-dimensional planetary environment, control its flight, monitor telemetry, and explore orbital trajectories.

The simulation integrates gravitational forces, atmospheric drag, fuel consumption, staging, orbital mechanics, sphere-of-influence transitions, and trajectory prediction. Users can also plan maneuvers and explore transfer opportunities between celestial bodies.

Orbital Architect 2D aims to make complex aerospace concepts more accessible through hands-on experimentation. By combining rocket engineering concepts with interactive orbital simulation, the project gives an educational environment where users can understand how spacecraft design decisions influence mission feasibility and navigation.
details:
Orbital Architect 2D is a browser-based rocket construction and orbital simulation platform built around three interconnected environments:

1.) Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB)

Users can design and assemble their own rockets using a selection of spacecraft components, including engines, fuel tanks, probe cores, decouplers, fairings, and scientific instruments.

The simulator evaluates the rocket's performance using aerospace calculations, including:

  • Delta-v: Estimates the total velocity change available from the rocket's propellant.
  • Thrust-to-weight ratio (TWR): Evaluates whether the rocket has sufficient thrust to overcome gravitational forces.
  • Mass calculations: Accounts for fuel, structural components, and individual rocket stages.
  • Engine performance: Uses engine thrust and specific impulse to estimate fuel consumption and propulsion capability.
  • Staging: Allows users to separate spent rocket stages during flight.

2.) Flight Simulation

After construction, users can launch their spacecraft into the planetary environment and control its flight.

The simulation includes:

  • Real-time rocket movement and gravitational acceleration.
  • Engine activation, throttle control, and manual steering.
  • Fuel consumption based on engine performance.
  • Multi-stage rocket separation.
  • Atmospheric drag and surface interactions.
  • Telemetry displaying altitude, velocity, orbital parameters, fuel, and other flight information.
  • Time acceleration to manage different phases of a mission.

3.) Orbital Navigation and Mission Planning

The orbital environment allows users to explore how spacecraft move under gravitational influence and plan potential trajectories.

Features include:

  • Predicted orbital trajectories and conic sections.
  • Apoapsis and periapsis calculations.
  • Planetary spheres of influence and celestial encounters.
  • Maneuver nodes for planning velocity changes.
  • Hohmann transfer approximations for orbital transfers.
  • A map interface displaying trajectories, orbital paths, celestial bodies, and planned maneuvers.

Scientific and Technical Foundation

The simulator incorporates established aerospace and orbital mechanics concepts, including the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, Newtonian gravitational acceleration, the thrust-to-weight ratio, and Keplerian orbital mechanics.

For orbital propagation, the simulation uses a combination of universal-variable Kepler propagation for coasting flight and fourth-order Runge-Kutta numerical integration for powered flight and atmospheric conditions.

The planetary environment and physical model are simplified and scaled for an accessible two-dimensional educational experience. The simulator is not intended for real-world spacecraft design or mission planning.

Key Benefits and Impact

  • Makes aerospace concepts interactive: Allows users to experiment with rocket construction, propulsion, staging, and orbital mechanics rather than only reading about them.
  • Connects engineering decisions to mission outcomes: Demonstrates how fuel capacity, engine selection, rocket mass, and thrust affect mission performance.
  • Encourages experimentation: Users can modify their designs, launch different configurations, and observe the resulting flight behavior
  • Introduces orbital mechanics: Makes concepts such as gravitational attraction, orbital transfers, maneuver planning, and planetary encounters more approachable.
  • Provides an accessible learning environment: Runs through a web browser and includes a dedicated How to Play guide to help new users understand the simulator.

Tools and Technologies

  • HTML5: Defines the structure of the simulator and supporting website.
  • CSS3: Handles the visual design, interface styling, animations, and responsive layouts.
  • JavaScript (ES6+): Powers rocket construction, physics calculations, orbital propagation, trajectory prediction, flight controls, and simulation logic.
  • Tailwind CSS: Supports interface styling and layout.
  • GitHub: Supports source-code management and collaboration.
  • Lovable: Used to help integrate the project systems.
  • Google Gemini: Assisted with interface layout and development.
  • ChatGPT: Used for troubleshooting code errors, debugging assistance, and technical problem-solving.

AI accelerated development, but the concept, features, direction, and final decisions remained team-led.

Creative Elements

  • A complete rocket-building environment connected to a playable flight simulator.
  • A two-dimensional planetary system that allows users to explore spacecraft movement and orbital transfers.
  • An integrated telemetry interface displaying mission performance in real time.
  • Interactive trajectory visualizations and maneuver planning.
  • A dedicated project website with a separate How to Play and Mission Guide page.
  • A consistent technical visual identity inspired by aerospace mission-control interfaces.
